PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Police Station — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches who works at the police station and how an officer helps — including the friendly version of the lost-child plan.

What is this?

A police station is where police officers work: they start their rounds here, keep lost things safe here, and help anyone who knocks, any hour.

What does it mean?

Keeping everyone safe is the idea — the badge means "you can ask me for help", and the station is where that promise lives.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know your own name and a grown-up&rsquo;s name — the two most powerful words in any lost moment. Officers know the rest.

Why this matters

Every town needs helpers who never sleep: while the town dreams, someone answers the phone, checks the streets, and walks the lost bicycle home.

What it teaches

Safety vocabulary (lost, helper, badge), the name-and-grown-up drill, trust in uniforms, and kind understanding of "people who work while we sleep".

Words to learn

policeofficerbadgestationsafelostfoundhelpuniform

Say this to your child

“"This is the police station — helpers work here, day and night. The badge means: you can ask me! If I am ever lost, I find an officer and say my name and my grown-up&rsquo;s name — and the helping begins."”

Step by step

  1. See the badge — a star on a shield — the same star officers wear on their chest and their patrol car.
  2. Officers start the day here: roll call, radio check, and off into the town.
  3. Lost things come here: bicycles, gloves, teddy bears — the shelf waits patiently.
  4. If a child is lost, the plan is simple and strong: find a police officer (or a parent with children), say your name and your grown-up&rsquo;s name, and stay together until found.
  5. The station never closes — somebody is there right now, tonight, and every night.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a star sits on a shield-shaped badge over the police station doors — the same design the officers carry, so a child can match the building to the helper.

Ask your child

"Who works at the police station?" (police officers) "What does the badge mean?" (you can ask me for help) "What do we say if we are lost?" (our name and our grown-up&rsquo;s name)

What your child can say or do

Your child might badge every drawing with a star and shield, radio the dinner table ("officer requesting snacks"), or practice the lost-plan on every walk — pointing out officers and whispering "helpers".

Out in the real world

In the US, UK and Canada the lost-child plan is the same: find a police officer or a parent with children and say your name. Practicing it as a game turns the scariest moment into a known routine — that is this card&rsquo;s whole job.

Try it together

The friendly-officer game: one toy walks a cushion street and gets "lost"; the officer asks kindly questions — name, who we are looking for — and walks everyone home. Reunion hug required by law.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who can we ask for help if we are lost?" (a police officer) "What do we tell them?" (our name and our grown-up&rsquo;s name)

This lesson pairs with the Police Station flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
